items.topic: Primary goal of the auth service
items.context: The item has no description. Vrooli already has scenario-authenticator (full JWT/OAuth/2FA/RBAC) and LPBS has its own independent auth. The auth service could mean many things — we need to clarify the core goal before anything else.

options.label: Unify existing auth into a shared identity service
options.rationale: Consolidate scenario-authenticator and LPBS auth into one service so all scenarios share a single user directory, SSO, and permission model. Highest impact but largest migration effort.

options.label: Create a shared auth middleware/library
options.rationale: Don't build a new service — extract common auth patterns (JWT validation, session management, RBAC) into a reusable Go package that scenarios import. Lower effort, keeps auth decentralized.

options.label: Integrate Keycloak as the central identity provider
options.rationale: Keycloak is already enabled as a resource. Wrap it with a thin Vrooli adapter so scenarios delegate auth to Keycloak. Gets enterprise SSO (SAML, OIDC) for free but adds operational complexity.

options.label: Extend scenario-authenticator to be the central auth service
options.rationale: scenario-authenticator already has most capabilities. Add cross-scenario token validation, service-to-service auth, and a shared user directory. Evolutionary approach, least throwaway work.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Describe your vision for the auth service

items.context: spec.json has no scope field set. This work could live as a new standalone scenario, extend an existing scenario, or be a cross-cutting library. Where should the code live?

options.label: New standalone scenario (scenarios/auth-service/)
options.rationale: Clean separation, own API/CLI/UI, independent lifecycle. Best if this becomes a core platform service.

options.label: Extend scenarios/scenario-authenticator/
options.rationale: Build on existing auth codebase. Avoids duplication but increases scope of that scenario.

options.label: Shared Go package (packages/auth/ or similar)
options.rationale: Library approach — no new scenario, just importable code. Best if goal is middleware/library (option B in d1).

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Specify a different location

items.context: Currently users exist independently in each scenario's database. A unified auth service needs a shared identity model.

options.label: Centralized user database with scenario-specific profiles
options.rationale: One users table owns identity (email, password, OAuth links). Each scenario stores its own user preferences/roles. Clean separation of identity vs. authorization.

options.label: Federated identity with token exchange
options.rationale: Each scenario keeps its user database but trusts tokens from the auth service. Less migration but eventual consistency challenges.

options.label: Keycloak-managed identity with SCIM provisioning
options.rationale: Keycloak owns user lifecycle, scenarios sync via SCIM. Enterprise-grade but higher complexity.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Describe your preferred identity model

items.context: How should scenarios verify that a user is authenticated? This is the core integration contract other scenarios will depend on.

options.label: Shared JWT with standard claims
options.rationale: Auth service issues JWTs with standardized claims (sub, roles, scopes). Scenarios validate locally using shared public key. Stateless, fast, well-understood.

options.label: Token introspection endpoint
options.rationale: Scenarios call auth service to validate opaque tokens. Centralizes validation logic but adds network hop and dependency.

options.label: Reverse proxy with auth sidecar
options.rationale: Auth handled at network layer before requests reach scenarios. Scenarios never see raw tokens. Cleanest integration but requires proxy infrastructure.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Describe your preferred mechanism

items.context: LPBS uses ad-hoc bearer tokens for inter-scenario calls. A standardized approach is needed for scenarios to securely call each other's APIs.

options.label: Mutual TLS (mTLS)
options.rationale: Certificate-based identity at transport layer. Very secure, no tokens to leak, but requires cert management infrastructure.

options.label: Service account JWTs with scope-based access
options.rationale: Each scenario gets a service account that can request scoped JWTs. Reuses existing JWT infrastructure, easy to audit.

options.label: API key registry with per-service permissions
options.rationale: Central registry of service API keys with allowlisted endpoints. Simple to implement but keys are long-lived secrets.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Describe your preferred approach

items.context: scenario-authenticator and LPBS both have live auth systems with users. How should existing users and sessions be handled during transition?

options.label: Big-bang migration with maintenance window
options.rationale: Migrate all users at once, switch over. Clean but requires downtime and coordination.

options.label: Dual-stack with gradual migration
options.rationale: New auth service runs alongside existing auth. Scenarios migrate one at a time. Old auth deprecated after all scenarios switch. Safest but longest timeline.

options.label: Defer migration — new scenarios only
options.rationale: Only new scenarios use the auth service. Existing scenarios keep their auth. Avoids migration risk but doesn't solve the unification problem.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Describe your preferred migration approach

items.text: scenario-authenticator already implements: JWT (RSA-signed, 60min default), OAuth2 (Google + GitHub), TOTP 2FA with backup codes, RBAC (admin/user roles), API key management, Redis-backed sessions with blacklisting, rate limiting, and full audit logging in PostgreSQL. This is a substantial foundation to build on rather than replace.

Keycloak is enabled as a Vrooli resource but completely unintegrated. It natively supports OIDC, SAML, social login, user federation (LDAP/AD), fine-grained authorization, and multi-tenancy. Adopting it would provide enterprise features for free but adds operational complexity (Java-based, resource-heavy).
